title: Resource Naming Conventions
description: Learn how to name API resources consistently using nouns, plural forms, and hierarchical relationships so your endpoints are predictable and self-documenting.

data.text: Good resource naming is one of the most important parts of API design. Clear, consistent names reduce the learning curve for consumers and make your API feel intuitive. In REST, URLs represent resources, so the naming convention directly affects how developers understand and interact with your API. When naming is inconsistent, clients waste time guessing patterns instead of building features, and support costs rise as teams ask why the API does not follow the expected structure.

RESTful URLs should identify resources using nouns. HTTP methods already describe actions, so repeating verbs in the URL is redundant and confusing. Favor simple, readable paths that describe what the resource is, not what the client wants to do. When you use verbs, you duplicate information and create an API that is harder to document and harder to learn. Developers expect GET to retrieve, POST to create, PUT to replace, and DELETE to remove. Keeping that contract clean lets them use standard tools and libraries without custom wrappers.

data.title: Good vs Bad Naming
data.content: Compare RESTful noun-based URLs with action-based URLs.
data.code:
BAD:
GET /getUsers
POST /createOrder
GET /deleteProduct/5

GOOD:
GET    /users
POST   /orders
DELETE /products/5

data.text: Collections are usually represented with plural nouns such as /users or /products. A specific item within a collection uses the singular form with an identifier: /users/42 or /products/42. This pattern makes the relationship between the collection and individual members explicit. Some teams prefer singular nouns, but consistency matters more than the specific choice. Once you pick a convention, apply it everywhere so the API feels like a single coherent system. Inconsistent pluralization is one of the most common complaints from API consumers.

data.title: Consistency Wins
data.text: Pick either plural or singular and stick with it across the entire API. Mixing styles forces consumers to guess the pattern for every new endpoint.

When resources have parent-child relationships, nest them in the URL path. For example, /users/42/orders shows orders that belong to user 42. Avoid nesting deeper than two levels. Deeply nested paths become brittle and harder to version, so consider query parameters for secondary filters instead. Deep nesting also creates tight coupling between resources, which makes independent deployment and scaling more difficult. If you find yourself needing three or more levels, rethink whether the relationship truly belongs in the path or if it should be expressed through filtering.

data.title: Hierarchical Resources
data.content: Express ownership through nesting, but keep it shallow.

terms.definition: An entity or object in your domain, identified by a URI.
A group of resources, such as /users.
Representing parent-child relationships in the URL path.

items.question: Should I use query parameters for filtering?
items.answer: Yes. Query parameters are ideal for optional filters, search queries, and pagination without changing the resource hierarchy.

items.question: How do I handle actions that are not CRUD operations?
items.answer: REST encourages mapping non-CRUD actions to resources. For example, /users/42/activate can represent an activation resource. When this feels forced, consider whether the action should be its own resource endpoint.

data.title: Takeaway
points: Use plural nouns for collections and singular nouns with IDs for individual items.
Avoid verbs in URLs because HTTP methods already describe actions.
Keep nesting shallow and use query parameters for filters.
data.takeaway: Predictable naming reduces friction for API consumers and makes your interface feel natural.
